Project Objectives 2.1 Mission of CUWP The central goal of CUWP was to enable low-cost technologies that sustainably upcycle plastic wastes. We also sought to develop the scientific and engineering workforce to enable the commercialization of plastic recycling technologies. The technology options for chemical recycling of plastics were experimentally validated at both the laboratory and pilot scale. Rigorous process models were developed for the different plastic recycling options using both historical data and experimental data that was collected in CUWP. We studied how material recovery facilities (MRFs) can be optimized to recycle different types of plastic wastes. The required purities for plastic wastes that are needed for chemical and mechanical recycling was developed. Thermal depolymerization of plastic wastes into a plastic-derived oil was done in both laboratory and pilot scale reactors. We analyzed the products of thermal depolymerization using modern analytical techniques. This experimental data was combined with first principal calculations to derive mechanistically based kinetic models for depolymerization of pure resins and mixed plastic streams. We studied how waxes and oils from the depolymerization of mixed waste plastics can be catalytically converted into olefins and aromatics in a fixed catalytic bed. We elucidated the relationship between catalyst properties and their performance. We developed rules for the maximum acceptable levels of polymer impurities (chlorine, nitrogen, other heteroatoms) in thermal depolymerization and catalytic upgrading. Technologies for removing these impurities were experimentally validated. Post-industrial plastic waste (PIW) multi-layer plastic films were recycled into their pure resin components using the STRAP process. Kilogram quantities of recycled resins were produced from STRAP and the mechanical properties were tested. New educational materials on plastic recycling were developed and classes were taught using this material at both the undergraduate and graduate level at CUWP partner universities, including Iowa State University, University of Guelph, Universidad Autonoma Metropolotina, Universidad Autonoma de San Luis Potosi, University of Massachusetts Amherst, and National Renewable Energy Laboratory. This curriculum material will be shared both inside and outside the institute. We hosted several summer research programs for undergraduate students on plastic recycling and held multiple seminar series dedicated to plastic recycling. Despite public support for plastics recycling, industry has struggled to make it commercially viable achieving only 2% recycling (The New Plastics Economy, 2016). The diversity of plastic wastes, the presence of contaminants, the large capital requirements, integration of the supply chain, and the difficulty of thoroughly depolymerizing plastics to their original monomers are significant challenges in upcycling waste plastics. Until these limitations are understood and a clear path forward identified, industry will be hesitant to invest in what might otherwise be viewed as early-stage research and development. The motivation of CUWP was to advance the science and engineering of plastic upcycling to the point where private investment is attractive and helps build the future workforce.
